newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Former Brazil president Franco mulls 1998 comeback.
newsitem.headline: Former Brazil president Franco mulls 1998 comeback.

text.p: Former Brazilian president Itamar Franco said Thursday he was considering running in next year's presidential race, but declined to openly declare his candidacy.

"I am a potential candidate for the presidency of the republic," Franco told a news conference, where he announced he was resigning from his post as Brazil's representative to the Organization of American States.
Franco, elected as vice president to Fernando Collor in 1989, took over the presidency in 1992 when Collor resigned amid a corruption scandal.

He has repeatedly hinted he would like to run for president in 1998 and claims he deserves the credit for the economic policies of the Real Plan, introduced by his then- finance minister, and now president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
Cardoso hopes Congress will approve a constitutional amendment allowing him to run for re-election next year.
Franco said he told Cardoso late Wednesday of their likely showdown and said the president had found his decision "understandable."
The former leader, who is not a member of any political party, said he would meet with left and right-wing parties to build a platform for his shot at the presidency.
"I can't be a candidate until I have a political party," he said.
Franco declined comment on what his campaign issues might be, but repeated his criticisms of the upcoming privatization of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and of Cardoso's re-election plan.
An survey published in March by the private Ibope polling company found Franco would win three percent of votes, compared to 46 percent for Cardoso if the latter was allowed to run for a second term.
Brazil's constitution currently prohibits presidents, state governors and mayors from seeking consecutive terms.
